newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria's Beecham targets the poor.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria's Beecham targets the poor.

text.p: Nigeria's largest drugs company Smithkline Beecham Nigeria (SB) said on Thursday it would introduce new products aimed at the bottom of the market.
"We will be broadening our consumer base in the new year as well as making our products more affordable," chief executive Jay Drosin told journalists in Lagos.
"The less priviledged .. are an area of the market we have never addressed in the past."
With over 100 million people Nigeria is Africa's most populous nation, but despite the country's crude oil wealth the bulk of the population lives in poverty.
SB will introduce oral rehydration salt into the market and cheap tests for the HIV virus which causes AIDS.
"Whereas the brand of the oral rehydration salt currently available in the country is being sold at 25 naira, ours will cost 10 naira," Drosin said.
He said the saliva card HIV test could give a result in 15 minutes to tell if somebody is infected with either HIV-I or HIV-II viruses.
Drosin said that after last month's merger with Sterling Products Nigeria the new company would enjoy economies of scale and increase profits despite Nigeria's cool economic climate.
"We have spent a year looking and dissecting this company, seeing what is wrong and what is right. We feel we have come up with the right solution," Drosin said.
Drosin said SB would expand into the West African market, launching products in both Ghana and Benin in 1997.
SB also hopes for a contract from the government's Petroleum Trust Fund, set up in 1994 to cushion the blow of fuel price increases through social spending.
Drosin said the company's fortunes in 1996 were hit by a prolonged port closure and high production costs.
Half-year profit after tax to end-June 1996 fell 10.5 percent to 68.6 million naira from 75.7 million naira in the same period of 1995.
